children.value: Check Your Understanding: Carrying Out a Complete Test

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Carrying Out a Complete Test

children.value: A city claims that 30% of its residents bike to work at least once a week. A local advocacy group suspects the true proportion is lower. In a random sample of 500 residents, 130 bike to work at least once a week.

model.question: Carry out step 1: what are the hypotheses?

choices.feedback: The suspicion is specifically that the rate is lower, so the alternative is one-sided.

model.hint: The claimed value is 0.30; the group suspects it is lower.

model.question: Carry out step 2: are the conditions met, and what is the test statistic?

choices.feedback: Check the standard error: $\sqrt{0.30 \times 0.70/500} \approx 0.0205$, so $z \approx -1.95$, not -0.04.
The conditions ARE met: $np_0 = 150$ and n(1 - $p_0) = 350$.

model.question: Steps 3 and 4: the p-value is P(Z $\leq -1.95) \approx 0.026$. Using $\alpha = 0.05$, what is the conclusion?

choices.text: Reject $H_0$—the data provide significant evidence that fewer than 30% of residents bike to work weekly
choices.feedback: Correct! Since $0.026 < 0.05$, we reject $H_0$ and conclude that fewer than 30% of residents bike to work weekly.

choices.text: Do not reject $H_0$—the evidence is not strong enough
choices.feedback: 0.026 is smaller than 0.05, so the results ARE significant.
The conclusion must be in context—about the proportion of residents who bike to work.

model.hint: Compare 0.026 with 0.05 and state the conclusion in context.

children.value: Before we move on to the next test, we use the z-test for proportions to bring up and illustrate some very important issues regarding hypothesis testing.
